name: Highway speed in SI units
statement: A car travels at $65$ miles per hour. One mile is exactly $1609.344$ m. Express this speed in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: multiply by conversion factors arranged so the unwanted units cancel. $65\,\text{mi/h}\times\frac{1609.344\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{mi}}\times\frac{1\ \text{h}}{3600\ \text{s}}=29.1$ m/s. A useful check: 1 m/s is about 2.24 mph.

name: Kilometers per hour to meters per second
statement: A train moves at $100$ km/h. What is its speed in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: $1$ km/h $=1000/3600$ m/s $=1/3.6$ m/s. So $100/3.6=27.8$ m/s. Dividing km/h by 3.6 is worth memorizing.

name: Bathtub volume in cubic meters
statement: A bathtub holds $150$ liters of water. One liter is $10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$. What is the volume in cubic meters?
solution: KEY IDEA: the liter is defined as a cubic decimeter, so $1\ \text{L}=10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$. Then $150\ \text{L}=0.150\ \text{m}^3$. That is a cube about $53$ cm on a side.

name: Density of water in SI units
statement: Water has density $1.00\ \text{g/cm}^3$. Express this in kg/m$^3$.
solution: KEY IDEA: $1\ \text{g}=10^{-3}$ kg and $1\ \text{cm}^3=10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3$, so the conversion factor is $10^{-3}/10^{-6}=10^{3}$. Hence $1.00\ \text{g/cm}^3=1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$.

name: Seconds in a year
statement: Take a year to be $365$ days. How many seconds are in one year?
solution: KEY IDEA: chain the conversions. $365\times24\times3600=3.15\times10^{7}$ s. The handy mnemonic is that a year is about $\pi\times10^{7}$ seconds.

name: Heartbeats in a lifetime
statement: A resting heart beats $70$ times per minute. Assuming that rate holds for a life of $80$ years ($365$ days each), how many times does the heart beat in a lifetime?
solution: KEY IDEA: convert the rate to beats per year, then multiply by the lifetime. $70\ \text{min}^{-1}\times5.26\times10^{5}\ \text{min/yr}=3.68\times10^{7}$ beats per year, and over $80$ years that is about $2.9\times10^{9}$ beats. A few billion beats is the right order of magnitude for most mammals.

name: Pendulum period from dimensional analysis
statement: The period of a simple pendulum can depend only on its length $L$, the gravitational field $g$, and its mass $m$. Dimensional analysis gives $T=k\sqrt{L/g}$, and the exact theory for small swings gives $k=2\pi$. Find the period of a pendulum of length $1.00$ m, with $g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
solution: KEY IDEA: mass cannot appear because no other quantity carries mass, and $\sqrt{L/g}$ is the only combination with units of time. Then $T=2\pi\sqrt{1.00/9.8}=2.01$ s. A one-meter pendulum ticking at about two seconds per swing is the origin of the old 'seconds pendulum'.

name: Significant figures in a product
statement: A rectangular plate is measured to be $2.50$ m by $3.1$ m. Report the area with the correct number of significant figures, in $\text{m}^2$.
solution: KEY IDEA: in a product, the result keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor. The raw product is $7.75\ \text{m}^2$, but $3.1$ has only two significant figures, so the area is $7.8\ \text{m}^2$.

name: Kilowatt-hour in joules
statement: Electric utilities bill energy in kilowatt-hours. How many joules are in $1.00$ kWh?
solution: KEY IDEA: energy is power times time, so $1\ \text{kWh}=1000\ \text{W}\times3600\ \text{s}=3.6\times10^{6}$ J. A watt is one joule per second, which makes the whole conversion one multiplication.

name: Light-year in meters
statement: Light travels at $2.998\times10^{8}$ m/s. Using a year of $365.25$ days, how many meters are in one light-year?
solution: KEY IDEA: a light-year is a distance, not a time: multiply speed by elapsed time. $2.998\times10^{8}\times3.156\times10^{7}=9.46\times10^{15}$ m.

name: Power of speed in the drag force
statement: At high speed the drag force on a car depends only on the air density $\rho$, the frontal area $A$, and the speed $v$: $F=C\rho^{a}A^{b}v^{c}$ with $C$ dimensionless. Find the exponent $c$.
solution: KEY IDEA: match powers of mass, length and time. $[\rho]=\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, $[A]=\text{m}^2$, $[v]=\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, and $[F]=\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$. Mass gives $a=1$; time gives $c=2$; length then gives $-3+2b+2=1$, so $b=1$. Drag therefore grows as the square of the speed, which is why highway fuel economy falls off so fast.

name: Wave speed on a guitar string
statement: A wave on a string travels at a speed set only by the tension $T$ and the mass per unit length $\mu$, with a dimensionless constant equal to $1$. A string is under $80.0$ N of tension and has $\mu=5.00\times10^{-3}$ kg/m. Find the wave speed.
solution: KEY IDEA: $[T/\mu]=(\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2})/(\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1})=\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}$, so $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ is the only speed you can build. Numerically $\sqrt{80.0/5.00\times10^{-3}}=\sqrt{1.60\times10^{4}}=126$ m/s.

name: Orbital period at four times the radius
statement: For circular orbits around the Sun, the period satisfies $T^2\propto r^3$. A comet orbits in a circle of radius four times the Earth's orbital radius. What is its period in years?
solution: KEY IDEA: $T\propto r^{3/2}$, so scaling $r$ by $4$ scales $T$ by $4^{3/2}=8$. The Earth's period is $1$ yr, so the comet takes $8$ yr. No constants are needed because you are taking a ratio.

name: Piano tuners in Chicago
statement: Estimate the number of full-time piano tuners in Chicago. Assume: population $2.7\times10^{6}$; $2.5$ people per household; one household in $20$ owns a piano; each piano is tuned once a year; a tuner services $4$ pianos a day for $250$ working days a year. How many tuners does the city support?
solution: KEY IDEA: compute the annual demand for tunings and divide by the annual output of one tuner. Households: $2.7\times10^{6}/2.5=1.08\times10^{6}$; pianos: $1.08\times10^{6}/20=5.4\times10^{4}$, so $5.4\times10^{4}$ tunings per year. One tuner does $4\times250=1000$ per year, giving $54$ tuners.

name: Counting raindrops
statement: A storm drops $2.5$ cm of rain on a $1.00\ \text{m}^2$ patch of ground. Model each raindrop as a sphere of radius $1.0$ mm. How many drops landed on that patch?
solution: KEY IDEA: total water volume divided by the volume of one drop. The rain volume is $1.00\ \text{m}^2\times0.025\ \text{m}=0.025\ \text{m}^3$, and one drop holds $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi(10^{-3})^3=4.19\times10^{-9}\ \text{m}^3$. The ratio is about $6.0\times10^{6}$ drops.

name: Atoms in a human body
statement: A person has a mass of $70$ kg. The body is mostly water and light elements; take the average mass per atom to be $7.0$ atomic mass units, with $1\ \text{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg. Estimate the number of atoms in the body.
solution: KEY IDEA: total mass divided by average mass per atom. One atom averages $7.0\times1.66\times10^{-27}=1.16\times10^{-26}$ kg, so $N=70/1.16\times10^{-26}\approx6.0\times10^{27}$ atoms. Water is 2 hydrogens (1 u) plus one oxygen (16 u) over 3 atoms, i.e. 6 u per atom, which is where the estimate comes from.

name: Power output of the Sun
statement: Sunlight arrives at the top of Earth's atmosphere with an intensity of $1361\ \text{W/m}^2$. The Earth-Sun distance is $1.50\times10^{11}$ m. Assuming the Sun radiates equally in all directions, what is its total power output?
solution: KEY IDEA: the power spreads uniformly over a sphere whose radius is the Earth-Sun distance, so $P=4\pi r^2 I$. That gives $4\pi(1.50\times10^{11})^2\times1361=3.85\times10^{26}$ W. Nothing about the Sun's interior is needed.

name: Gasoline burned by American cars
statement: Assume the United States has $2.5\times10^{8}$ cars, each driven $12{,}000$ miles a year at an average of $25$ miles per gallon. How many gallons of gasoline do they burn in a year?
solution: KEY IDEA: gallons per car per year is miles driven divided by miles per gallon. That is $12{,}000/25=480$ gallons per car, and $2.5\times10^{8}\times480=1.2\times10^{11}$ gallons a year.

name: Base units of the gravitational constant
statement: Newton's law of gravitation is $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$. Write the SI unit of $G$ as $\text{m}^{\alpha}\,\text{kg}^{\beta}\,\text{s}^{\gamma}$. What is $\beta$?
solution: KEY IDEA: solve for $G$ and read off the units. $G=Fr^2/(m_1m_2)$, so $[G]=(\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2})(\text{m}^2)/\text{kg}^2=\text{m}^3\text{kg}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}$. Hence $\beta=-1$.

name: Size of a copper atom from bulk density
statement: Copper has density $8960\ \text{kg/m}^3$ and molar mass $63.5$ g/mol. Avogadro's number is $6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. Treating each atom as occupying a small cube, estimate the edge length of that cube.
solution: KEY IDEA: one mole occupies $M/\rho$ of volume, so one atom occupies $M/(\rho N_A)$. That is $63.5\times10^{-3}/(8960\times6.022\times10^{23})=1.18\times10^{-29}\ \text{m}^3$, whose cube root is $2.3\times10^{-10}$ m. Atomic spacings of a couple of angstroms come out of any solid's density.

name: Reynolds number for a cyclist's arm
statement: The Reynolds number is $\mathrm{Re}=\rho v D/\mu$, where $\mu$ is the dynamic viscosity in $\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}$. For air take $\rho=1.2\ \text{kg/m}^3$ and $\mu=1.8\times10^{-5}\ \text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}$. Compute $\mathrm{Re}$ for a cylinder of diameter $0.10$ m moving at $10$ m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: $\mathrm{Re}$ is dimensionless, so the units must cancel; check that $\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}=\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ before trusting the number. Then $\mathrm{Re}=1.2\times10\times0.10/1.8\times10^{-5}=6.7\times10^{4}$, far above the value where flow becomes turbulent, which is why drag here scales as $v^2$ rather than $v$.

name: Filling a pool with a garden hose
statement: A garden hose has an inner diameter of $1.6$ cm and delivers water at $2.0$ m/s. How long does it take to fill a $1500$ L pool? Give the answer in minutes.
solution: KEY IDEA: volume flow rate is cross-sectional area times speed. $A=\pi(0.0080)^2=2.01\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$, so $Q=4.02\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$. Filling $1.50\ \text{m}^3$ takes $3.73\times10^{3}$ s, or $62$ min.

name: Speed of sound from dimensional analysis
statement: Sound in air travels at a speed built only from the ambient pressure $P$ and the density $\rho$, times a dimensionless factor. For an ideal gas that factor is $\sqrt{\gamma}$ with $\gamma=1.4$. Using $P=1.013\times10^{5}$ Pa and $\rho=1.29\ \text{kg/m}^3$, find the speed of sound.
solution: KEY IDEA: $[P/\rho]=(\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2})/(\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3})=\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}$, so $\sqrt{P/\rho}$ is the only available speed. With the factor $\sqrt{\gamma}$, $v=\sqrt{1.4\times1.013\times10^{5}/1.29}=332$ m/s, matching the measured value near $340$ m/s at room temperature.

name: Energy of a blast from its fireball
statement: The radius $R$ of a strong blast wave at time $t$ depends only on the released energy $E$ and the ambient air density $\rho$. Taking the dimensionless constant to be $1$, high-speed film shows a fireball of radius $100$ m at $t=15$ ms in air of density $1.25\ \text{kg/m}^3$. Estimate $E$.
solution: KEY IDEA: the only combination with units of length is $R=(Et^2/\rho)^{1/5}$, so $E=\rho R^5/t^2$. Substituting, $E=1.25\times(100)^5/(0.015)^2=5.6\times10^{13}$ J, roughly $13$ kilotons of TNT. G. I. Taylor famously used exactly this argument on published photographs to deduce the Trinity yield.

name: Energy released by a hurricane in a day
statement: A hurricane rains $1.5$ cm of water per day over a circular region of radius $300$ km. Condensing water releases latent heat $L=2.26\times10^{6}$ J/kg, and water has density $1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$. How much energy does the storm release in one day?
solution: KEY IDEA: every kilogram of rain that reaches the ground was first condensed from vapor, so the rainfall mass times $L$ is the heat released. Volume $=\pi(3.0\times10^{5})^2(0.015)=4.24\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^3$, mass $=4.24\times10^{12}$ kg, and $E=9.6\times10^{18}$ J. That is a few hundred times the daily electricity consumption of the entire world.

name: Terminal speed of a bigger hailstone
statement: Two hailstones have the same shape and density, but one has eight times the mass of the other. Drag is $F=\tfrac{1}{2}C\rho A v^2$ with the same $C$ for both. By what factor is the heavier stone's terminal speed larger?
solution: KEY IDEA: at terminal speed $mg=\tfrac12 C\rho Av^2$, so $v\propto\sqrt{m/A}$. Geometric similarity gives $m\propto L^3$ and $A\propto L^2$, so $v\propto\sqrt{L}$. Eight times the mass means twice the size, hence a speed ratio of $\sqrt{2}=1.41$.

name: Air molecules in a bedroom
statement: A bedroom measures $5.0\ \text{m}\times4.0\ \text{m}\times2.5\ \text{m}$. The air is at $1.013\times10^{5}$ Pa and $293$ K, and $k_B=1.381\times10^{-23}$ J/K. How many gas molecules does it contain?
solution: KEY IDEA: use $PV=Nk_BT$ rather than counting anything. The volume is $50\ \text{m}^3$, so $N=(1.013\times10^{5})(50)/(1.381\times10^{-23}\times293)=1.25\times10^{27}$ molecules. Equivalently, about $2000$ moles, since a mole of gas fills $24$ L at room conditions.

name: Building the Stefan-Boltzmann constant
statement: A blackbody radiates power per unit area $\sigma T^4$, where $\sigma$ is built from $k_B$, $\hbar$, and $c$ alone: $\sigma=A\,k_B^{p}\hbar^{q}c^{r}$ with $A$ dimensionless. Find $p$.
solution: KEY IDEA: $\sigma T^4$ must have units of $\text{W/m}^2$, and $T$ enters only through $k_BT$, an energy. So $\sigma T^4=A(k_BT)^4/(\hbar^3c^2)$ is forced, since $[\hbar^3c^2]$ carries exactly the leftover $\text{J}^4\text{m}^2/\text{W}$. Therefore $p=4$ (and $q=-3$, $r=-2$); the exact theory gives $A=\pi^2/60$.

name: The Planck length
statement: There is exactly one combination of $\hbar=1.0546\times10^{-34}\ \text{J}\cdot\text{s}$, $G=6.674\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}^3\text{kg}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}$, and $c=2.998\times10^{8}$ m/s with units of length. Compute it.
solution: KEY IDEA: write $\ell=\hbar^{a}G^{b}c^{d}$ and match M, L, T. Mass gives $a-b=0$, so $a=b$; the remaining two equations give $a=b=1/2$ and $d=-3/2$, i.e. $\ell_P=\sqrt{\hbar G/c^3}$. Numerically $\sqrt{1.0546\times10^{-34}\times6.674\times10^{-11}/(2.998\times10^{8})^3}=1.6\times10^{-35}$ m, some $20$ orders of magnitude below a proton.

name: Wavelength of a deep-water swell
statement: For waves on deep water, the speed can depend only on $g$ and the wavelength $\lambda$ (surface tension and depth are negligible here). The exact result carries a factor $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$: $v=\sqrt{g\lambda/2\pi}$. A swell is observed to travel at $15.0$ m/s. What is its wavelength? Use $g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
solution: KEY IDEA: $\sqrt{g\lambda}$ is the only speed you can form from $g$ and $\lambda$, so the wavelength must scale as $v^2/g$. Solving, $\lambda=2\pi v^2/g=2\pi(15.0)^2/9.8=144$ m. Long swells outrun short ones, which is why storm swell arrives sorted by wavelength.

name: Pulling a sled at an angle
statement: A child pulls a sled with a rope that makes an angle of $35^\circ$ above the horizontal. The tension in the rope is $240$ N. How large is the horizontal component of the rope's force, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: the component along an axis is the magnitude times the cosine of the angle to that axis. Here $F_x = F\cos\theta = (240\ \text{N})\cos 35^\circ = 197$ N. The vertical component, $240\sin 35^\circ = 138$ N, plays no role in this question.

name: Two-leg walk
statement: A hiker walks $4.0$ km due east, then $3.0$ km due north. What is the magnitude of her net displacement, in kilometres?
solution: KEY IDEA: displacements add as vectors, so add components and then take the magnitude. The net displacement is $(4.0\,\hat{\imath} + 3.0\,\hat{\jmath})$ km, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{4.0^2+3.0^2} = 5.0$ km. Note that this is less than the $7.0$ km of path length walked.

name: Work from a dot product
statement: A constant force $\vec{F} = (12\,\hat{\imath} - 5\,\hat{\jmath})$ N acts on a box while the box undergoes a displacement $\vec{d} = (3\,\hat{\imath} + 4\,\hat{\jmath})$ m. How much work does the force do, in joules?
solution: KEY IDEA: work is the dot product $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$, computed component by component. $W = (12)(3) + (-5)(4) = 36 - 20 = 16$ J. The force has a component opposing part of the motion, which is why the answer is much smaller than $|\vec F||\vec d| = 65$ J.

name: Angle between two pulls
statement: Two ropes pull on a ring. One exerts $\vec{A} = (3\,\hat{\imath} + 4\,\hat{\jmath})$ N and the other $\vec{B} = (4\,\hat{\imath} + 3\,\hat{\jmath})$ N. What is the angle between the two forces, in degrees?
solution: KEY IDEA: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{|\vec A||\vec B|}$. Here $\vec A\cdot\vec B = 12+12 = 24$ and $|\vec A| = |\vec B| = 5$, so $\cos\theta = 24/25 = 0.96$ and $\theta = 16.3^\circ$.

name: Length of a 3D displacement
statement: A drone flies from the origin to the point $(2, 3, 6)$ m. How far is it from the origin, in metres?
solution: KEY IDEA: the magnitude of a three-dimensional vector is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$. $\sqrt{4+9+36} = \sqrt{49} = 7.0$ m.

name: Vertical component of a launch
statement: A ball is thrown at $25$ m/s at an angle of $40^\circ$ above the horizontal. What is the vertical component of its initial velocity, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: the component perpendicular to the reference axis uses the sine. $v_y = (25\ \text{m/s})\sin 40^\circ = 16.1$ m/s. This is the piece that determines how high the ball rises.

name: Wrench on a bolt
statement: A mechanic pushes on a wrench with a force of $80$ N at a point $0.25$ m from the bolt. The force makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the wrench handle. What is the magnitude of the torque about the bolt, in N$\cdot$m?
solution: KEY IDEA: $|\vec\tau| = |\vec r\times\vec F| = rF\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the handle and the force. $\tau = (0.25)(80)\sin 60^\circ = 17.3$ N$\cdot$m. Only the component of $\vec F$ perpendicular to the handle twists the bolt.

name: Making two vectors perpendicular
statement: For what value of $k$ are the vectors $\vec{A} = 3\,\hat{\imath} + k\,\hat{\jmath} - 2\,\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 4\,\hat{\imath} + 5\,\hat{\jmath} + 1\,\hat{k}$ perpendicular? Give the value of $k$ (dimensionless).
solution: KEY IDEA: two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product vanishes. $\vec A\cdot\vec B = 12 + 5k - 2 = 0$, so $5k = -10$ and $k = -2$.

name: Drifting across a river
statement: A boat points straight across a river and moves at $4.0$ m/s relative to the water. The river current is $3.0$ m/s downstream. What is the boat's speed relative to the bank, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: velocities add as vectors: $\vec v_{bank} = \vec v_{water} + \vec v_{current}$. The two are perpendicular, so the speed is $\sqrt{4.0^2 + 3.0^2} = 5.0$ m/s.

name: Change of velocity around a corner
statement: A car travelling at $12$ m/s due east turns and ends up travelling at $12$ m/s due north, without changing speed. What is the magnitude of its change in velocity, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: $\Delta\vec v = \vec v_f - \vec v_i$ is a vector difference, not a difference of speeds. With $\vec v_i = 12\,\hat{\imath}$ and $\vec v_f = 12\,\hat{\jmath}$, $\Delta\vec v = (-12\,\hat{\imath} + 12\,\hat{\jmath})$ m/s, of magnitude $12\sqrt2 = 17$ m/s. The speed is unchanged but the velocity certainly is not.

name: Component along a diagonal
statement: A force $\vec{F} = (5\,\hat{\imath} + 12\,\hat{\jmath})$ N acts on a bead that is constrained to slide along a wire pointing in the direction $\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath}$. What is the component of $\vec F$ along the wire, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: the component of $\vec F$ along a direction is $\vec F\cdot\hat u$, where $\hat u$ is a unit vector. Here $\hat u = (\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath})/\sqrt2$, so $\vec F\cdot\hat u = (5+12)/\sqrt2 = 17/\sqrt2 = 12.0$ N. Forgetting to normalise $\hat u$ is the usual mistake.

name: Steering to land straight across
statement: A river $80$ m wide flows at $2.0$ m/s. A swimmer can swim at $5.0$ m/s relative to the water and wants to land at the point directly opposite her starting point. At what angle upstream from the straight-across direction must she aim, in degrees?
solution: KEY IDEA: to have zero net downstream velocity, the upstream component of her swimming velocity must cancel the current. That requires $v\sin\theta = u$, so $\sin\theta = 2.0/5.0 = 0.40$ and $\theta = 23.6^\circ$. The width of the river does not affect the aiming angle, only the crossing time.

name: Plane in a crosswind
statement: A small plane holds a heading due north with an airspeed of $180$ km/h. A steady wind of $50$ km/h blows from the west toward the east. What is the plane's ground speed, in km/h?
solution: KEY IDEA: ground velocity = air velocity + wind velocity, and here the two are perpendicular. The ground velocity is $(50\,\hat{\imath} + 180\,\hat{\jmath})$ km/h, so the ground speed is $\sqrt{50^2+180^2} = 187$ km/h. The plane is also blown $50$ km/h off course to the east.

name: Area of a triangular plate
statement: A flat triangular plate has corners at $A = (0,0,0)$, $B = (2,3,1)$ and $C = (1,-1,4)$, with coordinates in metres. What is the area of the plate, in m$^2$?
solution: KEY IDEA: the magnitude of a cross product is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors, so a triangle has area $\tfrac12|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|$. Here $\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC} = (13, -7, -5)$, whose magnitude is $15.59$, giving an area of $7.79$ m$^2$.

name: Magnetic force on an ion
statement: An ion of charge $q = +2.0\ \mu$C moves with velocity $\vec v = 3.0\times10^{5}\,\hat{\imath}$ m/s through a magnetic field $\vec B = (0.50\,\hat{\jmath} + 0.20\,\hat{k})$ T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: $\vec F = q\,\vec v\times\vec B$. With $\vec v$ along $\hat{\imath}$, $\vec v\times\vec B = 3.0\times10^{5}(0.50\,\hat{k} - 0.20\,\hat{\jmath})$, of magnitude $1.616\times10^{5}$ m$\cdot$T/s. Multiplying by $q = 2.0\times10^{-6}$ C gives $F = 0.323$ N.

name: Torque from a 3D position vector
statement: A force $\vec F = 50\,\hat{k}$ N is applied at the point $\vec r = (0.30\,\hat{\imath} + 0.20\,\hat{\jmath})$ m relative to a pivot. What is the magnitude of the torque about the pivot, in N$\cdot$m?
solution: KEY IDEA: compute $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ component by component. $\vec\tau = (0.20)(50)\,\hat{\imath} - (0.30)(50)\,\hat{\jmath} = (10\,\hat{\imath} - 15\,\hat{\jmath})$ N$\cdot$m, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{10^2+15^2} = 18.0$ N$\cdot$m.

name: Third force for equilibrium
statement: Three forces act on a small ring and hold it in equilibrium. One is $30$ N pointing along the $+x$ axis; another is $40$ N pointing $120^\circ$ counterclockwise from the $+x$ axis. What is the magnitude of the third force, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: in equilibrium the three forces sum to zero, so the third equals the negative of the sum of the first two. The first two add to $(30 - 20)\,\hat{\imath} + 34.64\,\hat{\jmath} = (10, 34.64)$ N, so the third has magnitude $\sqrt{10^2 + 34.64^2} = 36.1$ N.

name: Angle to the vertical
statement: A cable pulls in the direction $\vec v = (4\,\hat{\imath} - 3\,\hat{\jmath} + 12\,\hat{k})$, where $\hat k$ points vertically upward. What angle does the cable make with the vertical, in degrees?
solution: KEY IDEA: the direction cosine with respect to an axis is the component along that axis divided by the magnitude. $|\vec v| = \sqrt{16+9+144} = 13$, so $\cos\theta = 12/13$ and $\theta = 22.6^\circ$.

name: Volume of a slanted box
statement: A parallelepiped is spanned by the edge vectors $\vec a = (2,1,0)$ m, $\vec b = (0,3,1)$ m and $\vec c = (1,0,4)$ m. What is its volume, in m$^3$?
solution: KEY IDEA: the volume is the absolute value of the scalar triple product $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$. Here $\vec b\times\vec c = (12, 1, -3)$, so $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c) = 24 + 1 + 0 = 25$, giving $25$ m$^3$.

name: Diagonal of a cube
statement: A crystal has a cubic unit cell. What angle does the body diagonal of a cube make with one of the cube's edges, in degrees?
solution: KEY IDEA: take the cube of side $1$ with an edge along $\hat{\imath}$ and the diagonal along $(1,1,1)$. Then $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\theta = 54.7^\circ$. Every edge meeting that corner makes the same angle with the diagonal.

name: Work done by gravity on a ramp
statement: A $25$ kg crate slides $8.0$ m down a ramp inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. How much work does gravity do on the crate, in joules?
solution: KEY IDEA: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d = mgd\cos\phi$, where $\phi = 60^\circ$ is the angle between the downward weight and the displacement along the ramp. Equivalently, only the drop in height matters: $W = mgd\sin 30^\circ = (25)(9.8)(8.0)(0.50) = 980$ J.

name: Two forces at an angle
statement: Two forces of $12$ N and $18$ N act at the same point with an angle of $50^\circ$ between them. What is the magnitude of their resultant, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: $|\vec A + \vec B|^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta$, which follows from expanding the dot product of the sum with itself. Here $144 + 324 + 2(12)(18)\cos 50^\circ = 745.7$, so the resultant is $27.3$ N.

name: Crossing against a fast current
statement: A river $150$ m wide flows at $3.0$ m/s. A rower can row at only $2.0$ m/s relative to the water, so she cannot avoid being carried downstream. If she chooses her heading to make the downstream drift as small as possible, how far downstream does she land, in metres?
solution: KEY IDEA: with the boat slower than the current, minimise the drift-to-width ratio rather than the drift itself. If she aims at angle $\theta$ upstream of straight across, the crossing time is $w/(v\cos\theta)$ and the drift is $x = w\dfrac{u - v\sin\theta}{v\cos\theta}$. Setting $dx/d\theta = 0$ gives $\sin\theta = v/u = 2/3$, and substituting back gives $x = w\sqrt{u^2 - v^2}/v = 150\sqrt{5}/2 = 168$ m.

name: The perpendicular leftover
statement: A force $\vec F = (3\,\hat{\imath} + 4\,\hat{\jmath})$ N acts on a bead threaded on a straight rod pointing along $\vec d = (1,2,2)$. The rod exerts whatever transverse force is needed to keep the bead on it. What is the magnitude of the component of $\vec F$ perpendicular to the rod, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: split $\vec F$ into a piece parallel to $\hat d$ and the leftover. With $\hat d = (1,2,2)/3$, the parallel component is $\vec F\cdot\hat d = (3 + 8)/3 = 3.667$ N. Since $|\vec F| = 5$ N and the two pieces are perpendicular, the transverse part is $\sqrt{5^2 - 3.667^2} = 3.40$ N.

name: Closest approach of two ships
statement: At noon, ship B is $12$ km due east of ship A. Ship A steams east at $18$ km/h; ship B steams north at $10$ km/h. Treating both as points moving in straight lines, what is their distance of closest approach, in kilometres?
solution: KEY IDEA: work in A's frame. The relative position of B is $\vec r_0 = (12, 0)$ km and the relative velocity is $\vec v_{rel} = (10\,\hat{\jmath}) - (18\,\hat{\imath}) = (-18, 10)$ km/h. The closest approach is the perpendicular distance from A to that straight line, $d = |\vec r_0\times\vec v_{rel}|/|\vec v_{rel}| = 120/20.59 = 5.83$ km, reached after about $0.51$ h.

name: Pushing a crate up a slope
statement: A $40$ kg crate rests on a frictionless ramp inclined at $25^\circ$. A worker pushes it with a $200$ N force directed horizontally, into the hill. What is the net force on the crate along the ramp surface, in newtons? Take a positive answer to mean the crate accelerates up the slope.
solution: KEY IDEA: resolve both the horizontal push and the vertical weight along the ramp direction. The push contributes $200\cos 25^\circ = 181.3$ N up the slope; gravity contributes $mg\sin 25^\circ = (40)(9.8)\sin 25^\circ = 165.7$ N down the slope. The net along-ramp force is $181.3 - 165.7 = 15.6$ N, just barely up the slope.

name: Area of a parallelogram in space
statement: A flat solar panel is a parallelogram whose adjacent sides are $\vec a = (4, -2, 1)$ m and $\vec b = (1, 3, 2)$ m. What is the area of the panel, in m$^2$?
solution: KEY IDEA: the area of the parallelogram is $|\vec a\times\vec b|$. Computing, $\vec a\times\vec b = (-2\cdot2 - 1\cdot3,\ 1\cdot1 - 4\cdot2,\ 4\cdot3 + 2\cdot1) = (-7, -7, 14)$, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{49+49+196} = 17.1$ m$^2$.

name: Proton in a general field
statement: A proton ($q = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) moves with velocity $\vec v = (2.0\,\hat{\imath} - 1.0\,\hat{\jmath} + 3.0\,\hat{k})\times10^{6}$ m/s in a magnetic field $\vec B = (0.050\,\hat{\imath} + 0.10\,\hat{\jmath} - 0.020\,\hat{k})$ T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: evaluate $\vec v\times\vec B$ by the determinant rule, then multiply by $q$. The cross product is $(-0.28, 0.19, 0.25)\times10^{6}$ in SI units, of magnitude $4.207\times10^{5}$. Multiplying by $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C gives $F = 6.73\times10^{-14}$ N.

name: Impact parameter of an alpha particle
statement: At a certain instant an alpha particle is at position $\vec r_0 = (3.0\,\hat{\imath} - 4.0\,\hat{\jmath} + 2.0\,\hat{k})\times10^{-12}$ m relative to a heavy nucleus, moving with velocity $\vec v = (2.0\,\hat{\imath} + 1.0\,\hat{\jmath} - 2.0\,\hat{k})\times10^{6}$ m/s. If the particle were undeflected and continued in a straight line, how close would it come to the nucleus, in metres?
solution: KEY IDEA: the impact parameter is the perpendicular distance from the nucleus to the straight-line path, and $|\vec r_0\times\vec v| = |\vec r_0||\vec v|\sin\theta$ picks out exactly the perpendicular piece. So $b = |\vec r_0\times\vec v|/|\vec v|$. Here $\vec r_0\times\vec v = (6.0, 10.0, 11.0)\times10^{-6}$ in SI units, of magnitude $1.603\times10^{-5}$, and $|\vec v| = 3.0\times10^{6}$ m/s, giving $b = 5.34\times10^{-12}$ m. Since $\vec r_0\cdot\vec v < 0$, the particle is still approaching, so this distance is actually reached.

name: Three cables holding a lamp
statement: A $500$ N lamp hangs at the point $P = (0,0,0)$ and is held up by three straight cables running to ceiling anchors at $A = (2, 0, 3)$ m, $B = (-1, 2, 3)$ m and $C = (-1, -2, 3)$ m. What is the tension in cable $PA$, in newtons?
solution: KEY IDEA: each cable pulls along its own unit vector, and the three tensions plus the weight must sum to zero. Writing $\hat u_A = (2,0,3)/\sqrt{13}$, $\hat u_B = (-1,2,3)/\sqrt{14}$, $\hat u_C = (-1,-2,3)/\sqrt{14}$, the condition $T_A\hat u_A + T_B\hat u_B + T_C\hat u_C = 500\,\hat k$ gives three equations. Symmetry in $y$ forces $T_B = T_C$, and solving the remaining $x$ and $z$ equations gives $T_A = 200$ N (with $T_B = T_C = 208$ N).

name: Velocity from a quadratic position
statement: A cart moves along a straight track. Its position in meters is $x(t) = 3t^2 - 4t + 2$, with $t$ in seconds. Find the speed of the cart at $t = 3\,\mathrm{s}$, in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: velocity is the time derivative of position. $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 6t - 4$. At $t = 3\,\mathrm{s}$, $v = 18 - 4 = 14\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Acceleration from a cubic position
statement: A bead slides on a wire with position $x(t) = 5t^3 - 2t$ (meters, seconds). Find its acceleration at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: KEY IDEA: acceleration is the second derivative of position. $v = 15t^2 - 2$ and $a = 30t$. At $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, $a = 60\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Top of the ball's flight
statement: A ball is thrown straight up from the ground. Its height in meters is $y(t) = 20t - 4.9t^2$. How long after launch does it reach its highest point, in seconds?
solution: KEY IDEA: at the top of the flight the velocity is zero, so set $dy/dt = 0$. $v = 20 - 9.8t = 0$ gives $t = 20/9.8 = 2.04\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: When does the acceleration vanish?
statement: A particle's velocity in m/s is $v(t) = 8t - 3t^2$. At what time is its acceleration zero, in seconds?
solution: KEY IDEA: $a = dv/dt$. Here $a = 8 - 6t$, which is zero at $t = 8/6 = 1.33\,\mathrm{s}$. This is also the instant the particle is moving fastest.

name: Fastest point of an oscillation
statement: A mass on a spring oscillates with $x(t) = 0.50\sin(4.0t)$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds. Find its maximum speed, in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: differentiate and read off the amplitude of the result. $v = (0.50)(4.0)\cos(4.0t) = 2.0\cos(4.0t)$, so the largest speed is $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, reached whenever the mass passes through $x = 0$.

name: How far out does it get?
statement: A trolley moves with $x(t) = 12t - t^3$ (meters, seconds), starting at the origin at $t=0$. Find the largest positive value of $x$ it reaches, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: the turning point is where $v = 0$. $v = 12 - 3t^2 = 0$ gives $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$. Then $x = 12(2) - 2^3 = 16\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: Braking with exponential decay
statement: A boat's engine is cut and its speed decays as $v(t) = 30e^{-t/5}$ m/s, with $t$ in seconds. Find its acceleration at $t = 0$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (report the signed value).
solution: KEY IDEA: differentiate the exponential using the chain rule. $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = 30\left(-\tfrac{1}{5}\right)e^{-t/5} = -6e^{-t/5}$. At $t = 0$ this is $-6.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Speed on a circular track
statement: A stone is whirled on a string of radius $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$. Its angle from the $x$-axis is $\theta(t) = 0.50t^2$ radians. Find the stone's speed at $t = 4.0\,\mathrm{s}$, in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: for circular motion $v = R\,\frac{d\theta}{dt}$. Here $\dot\theta = t$, so at $t = 4.0\,\mathrm{s}$, $\dot\theta = 4.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and $v = (3.0)(4.0) = 12\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Inflating balloon
statement: A spherical weather balloon is being inflated. At the moment its radius is $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$, the radius is growing at $0.020\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How fast is the volume increasing at that moment, in $\mathrm{m^3/s}$?
solution: KEY IDEA: related rates through the chain rule. $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so $\frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 \frac{dr}{dt} = 4\pi (0.50)^2 (0.020) = 0.0628\,\mathrm{m^3/s}$.

name: Tip of a walking shadow
statement: A street lamp holds a bulb $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ above level ground. A person $1.8\,\mathrm{m}$ tall walks away from the base of the lamp at $1.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How fast does the tip of the person's shadow move along the ground, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: similar triangles give a linear relation, then differentiate. If $x$ is the person's distance from the lamp and $s$ the shadow tip's distance, $\frac{1.8}{5.0} = \frac{s-x}{s}$, so $s = \frac{5.0}{5.0-1.8}x$. Differentiating, $\dot s = \frac{5.0}{3.2}(1.5) = 2.34\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Ladder sliding down a wall
statement: A $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its base is dragged away from the wall at a steady $0.40\,\mathrm{m/s}$. When the base is $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ from the wall, how fast is the top sliding down, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: differentiate the constraint $x^2 + y^2 = L^2$. This gives $x\dot x + y\dot y = 0$, so $\dot y = -x\dot x/y$. With $x = 3.0$, $y = \sqrt{25-9} = 4.0$, and $\dot x = 0.40$, the top moves down at $(3.0)(0.40)/4.0 = 0.30\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Acceleration from a speed-position graph
statement: A puck slides so that its speed depends on position as $v = 2.0\sqrt{x}$, with $v$ in m/s and $x$ in meters. Find its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: KEY IDEA: when speed is known as a function of position, use $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$. Here $\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1.0}{\sqrt{x}}$, so $a = 2.0\sqrt{x}\cdot\frac{1.0}{\sqrt{x}} = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The motion is uniformly accelerated, which matches $v^2 = 2ax$.

name: Rocket at peak acceleration change
statement: A small rocket rises with velocity $v(t) = 500\ln\!\left(1 + \frac{t}{20}\right) - 9.8t$ m/s, where $t$ is in seconds. At what time is its acceleration zero, in seconds?
solution: KEY IDEA: differentiate with the chain rule and set the result to zero. $a = \frac{500}{20+t} - 9.8 = 0$ gives $20 + t = \frac{500}{9.8} = 51.0$, so $t = 31.0\,\mathrm{s}$. This is when the rocket is moving fastest.

name: Winching a boat to the dock
statement: A winch on a dock sits $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ above the point where a rope is tied to a boat's bow. The rope is reeled in at $0.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$. When $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ of rope remain between winch and bow, how fast is the boat approaching the dock, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: with $x$ the horizontal distance and $L$ the rope length, $x^2 + 2.0^2 = L^2$, so $x\dot x = L\dot L$. When $L = 5.0$, $x = \sqrt{25-4} = 4.583\,\mathrm{m}$, giving $\dot x = (5.0)(0.50)/4.583 = 0.546\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The boat moves faster than the rope is pulled.

name: Half-amplitude time of a damped swing
statement: A pendulum's swing amplitude decays as $A(t) = A_0 e^{-t/4.0}$, with $t$ in seconds. How long does it take the amplitude to fall to half its initial value, in seconds?
solution: KEY IDEA: the decay constant sets the rate, since $\frac{dA}{dt} = -A/4.0$. Solving $e^{-t/4.0} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ gives $t = 4.0\ln 2 = 2.77\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: Closest approach of two cars
statement: At $t = 0$ a car leaves an intersection heading east at a constant $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. At the same moment a second car is $100\,\mathrm{m}$ north of the intersection, heading south toward it at a constant $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the smallest distance between the two cars, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: minimize the squared separation, which avoids differentiating a square root. $D^2 = (20t)^2 + (100-15t)^2$; setting $\frac{d(D^2)}{dt} = 1250t - 3000 = 0$ gives $t = 2.4\,\mathrm{s}$. Then the separations are $48\,\mathrm{m}$ east and $64\,\mathrm{m}$ north, so $D = 80\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: Speed for maximum engine power
statement: A motor pushes a sled with a force that drops with speed: $F = 4000 - 20v$ newtons, with $v$ in m/s. Find the maximum mechanical power the motor can deliver, in watts.
solution: KEY IDEA: $P = Fv$, so maximize $P(v) = 4000v - 20v^2$. Setting $\frac{dP}{dv} = 4000 - 40v = 0$ gives $v = 100\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $P = (4000-2000)(100) = 2.0\times 10^5\,\mathrm{W}$.

name: Equilibrium from a potential well
statement: Two atoms interact with potential energy $U(x) = \frac{6.0}{x^2} - \frac{4.0}{x}$, where $U$ is in joules and $x$ is the separation in meters. Find the separation at which the atoms are in equilibrium, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: the force is $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$, and equilibrium means $\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$. Here $\frac{dU}{dx} = -\frac{12}{x^3} + \frac{4.0}{x^2} = 0$, so $x = 12/4.0 = 3.0\,\mathrm{m}$. Since $U$ has a minimum there, the equilibrium is stable.

name: Lifeguard's fastest route
statement: A lifeguard stands on sand $40\,\mathrm{m}$ from a straight shoreline. A swimmer in trouble is $30\,\mathrm{m}$ out into the water, and $100\,\mathrm{m}$ down the beach measured parallel to the shoreline. The lifeguard runs at $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ on sand and swims at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the shortest possible time to reach the swimmer, in seconds.
solution: KEY IDEA: let the lifeguard enter the water a distance $x$ down the beach and minimize $T(x) = \frac{\sqrt{40^2+x^2}}{6.0} + \frac{\sqrt{30^2+(100-x)^2}}{2.0}$. Setting $dT/dx = 0$ is exactly Snell's law, $\frac{\sin\theta_1}{6.0} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{2.0}$, and gives $x = 90.4\,\mathrm{m}$. The resulting time is $32.2\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: Rate of change of speed
statement: A drone's velocity components in m/s are $v_x = 3.0 + 2.0t$ and $v_y = 4.0$, with $t$ in seconds. How fast is its speed increasing at $t = 0$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$?
solution: KEY IDEA: the rate of change of speed is not the magnitude of the acceleration. Differentiating $|\vec v| = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$ gives $\frac{d|\vec v|}{dt} = \frac{v_x a_x + v_y a_y}{|\vec v|}$. At $t=0$: $|\vec v| = 5.0$, $a_x = 2.0$, $a_y = 0$, so the answer is $(3.0)(2.0)/5.0 = 1.2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, less than $|\vec a| = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Fastest point on a rolling tire
statement: A bicycle wheel rolls without slipping along a road while the bicycle moves at $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Consider a small pebble stuck in the tread. Find the largest speed the pebble ever has relative to the road, in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: superpose translation and rotation. A tread point has position $x = v t + R\sin(\ldots)$ type terms; differentiating the cycloid gives speed $2v\left|\sin\frac{\phi}{2}\right|$, where $\phi$ is the angle turned since the point touched the road. The maximum is $2v = 16\,\mathrm{m/s}$, at the top of the wheel; the bottom point is instantaneously at rest.

name: Drag that depends on position
statement: A dart fired into a thick gel slows according to $v(x) = 20e^{-0.050x}$, where $v$ is in m/s and $x$ is the depth in meters. Find its acceleration at depth $x = 10\,\mathrm{m}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (report the signed value).
solution: KEY IDEA: use $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ because speed is given versus position. $\frac{dv}{dx} = -1.0e^{-0.050x}$, so $a = -20e^{-0.10x}$. At $x = 10\,\mathrm{m}$, $a = -20e^{-1} = -7.36\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Acceleration of the ladder's top
statement: A $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ ladder leans against a vertical wall, and its base is dragged away from the wall at a constant $0.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$. When the base is $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ from the wall, find the magnitude of the acceleration of the ladder's top, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: KEY IDEA: differentiate the constraint twice. From $y = \sqrt{L^2-x^2}$, $\dot y = -x\dot x/y$, and differentiating again with $\ddot x = 0$ gives $\ddot y = -\frac{\dot x^2}{y} + \frac{x\dot x\,\dot y}{y^2}$. With $x=3.0$, $y=4.0$, $\dot x = 0.60$, $\dot y = -0.45$: $\ddot y = -0.090 - 0.0506 = -0.141\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, so the magnitude is $0.141\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Best throwing angle off a cliff
statement: A stone is thrown at $25\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from the edge of a cliff $30\,\mathrm{m}$ above flat ground. Choosing the launch angle to make the stone land as far from the base of the cliff as possible, find that maximum horizontal distance, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: write the range as a function of the launch angle and maximize it. Flight time comes from $-30 = v_0\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac12 g t^2$, and $R(\theta) = v_0\cos\theta\,t$. Setting $dR/d\theta = 0$ gives $\theta = 35.7^\circ$, below $45^\circ$ because the extra drop rewards a flatter, faster horizontal throw. The maximum range is $R = 88.8\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: When does the projectile stop receding?
statement: A ball is launched from the origin at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $80^\circ$ above the horizontal. Its straight-line distance from the launch point does not increase monotonically. Find the first time at which that distance stops increasing, in seconds.
solution: KEY IDEA: the distance $r$ stops growing when $\frac{d(r^2)}{dt} = 2\vec r\cdot\vec v = 0$, i.e. when velocity is perpendicular to the position vector. With $x = v_0\cos\theta\,t$ and $y = v_0\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac12 g t^2$, dividing out the trivial root $t=0$ and solving gives $t = 2.14\,\mathrm{s}$. This happens only for steep launches, $\theta > 70.5^\circ$.

name: Chain sliding off a table
statement: A uniform chain of length $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ lies on a frictionless table with $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ hanging over the edge. Released from rest, how fast is the chain moving at the instant the last link leaves the table, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: with $x$ the hanging length, the driving weight is $Mgx/L$ on total mass $M$, so $a = gx/L$. Write $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ and integrate: $\tfrac12 v^2 = \frac{g}{2L}(L^2 - x_0^2)$. Thus $v = \sqrt{gL\left(1 - x_0^2/L^2\right)} = \sqrt{(9.8)(2.0)(1-0.0625)} = 4.29\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Longest shot up a slope
statement: A ball is projected at $14\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from a point on a hillside that rises at $20^\circ$ to the horizontal. Choosing the launch direction to maximize the distance the ball travels along the slope before landing on it, find that maximum distance, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: in axes tilted with the slope, the range along the incline is $R(\theta) = \frac{2v_0^2\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\alpha)}{g\cos^2\alpha}$ measured from the horizontal launch angle $\theta$. Differentiating, the product of sines and cosines peaks at $\theta = 45^\circ + \alpha/2 = 55^\circ$, and then $R_{\max} = \frac{v_0^2}{g(1+\sin\alpha)} = \frac{196}{9.8(1.342)} = 14.9\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: Total acceleration on a banked oval
statement: A car starts a lap on a circular track of radius $200\,\mathrm{m}$ at $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and speeds up steadily, its speed being $v(t) = 5.0 + 0.80t$ m/s. At what time does the magnitude of its total acceleration first reach $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, in seconds?
solution: KEY IDEA: the tangential part is $dv/dt = 0.80\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and the centripetal part is $v^2/R$, and they are perpendicular. Setting $\sqrt{0.80^2 + (v^2/200)^2} = 2.0$ gives $v^2 = 200\sqrt{4.0-0.64} = 366.7$, so $v = 19.1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $t = (19.1-5.0)/0.80 = 17.7\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: Fastest-turning telescope
statement: A rocket lifts off from rest straight up with a constant acceleration of $20\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. An observer stands $800\,\mathrm{m}$ from the launch pad and tracks it with a telescope. Find the maximum rate at which the telescope's elevation angle must turn, in rad/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: with $y = 10t^2$ and $\tan\theta = y/800$, the chain rule gives $\dot\theta = \frac{800\,\dot y}{800^2 + y^2} = \frac{16000t}{640000 + 100t^4}$. Setting $d\dot\theta/dt = 0$ gives $300t^4 = 640000$, so $t = 6.80\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\dot\theta = 0.127\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Unlike the constant-speed case, the peak is not at liftoff, because the rocket starts too slow.

name: Cheapest shot to a target
statement: A cannon must hit a target that sits $40\,\mathrm{m}$ horizontally away and $15\,\mathrm{m}$ above the muzzle. Find the smallest launch speed that can reach the target, in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: eliminate time to get the trajectory $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}\sec^2\theta$, then solve for $v_0^2$ as a function of $\theta$ and minimize it. Differentiating gives the condition $\tan 2\theta = -x/y$, and substituting back yields the clean result $v_{\min}^2 = g\left(y + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right)$. With $x = 40$, $y = 15$: $v_{\min} = \sqrt{9.8(15+42.7)} = 23.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Trapezoid on a velocity-time graph
statement: A train starts from rest. Its velocity rises linearly from $0$ to $12$ m/s during the first $4$ s, stays at $12$ m/s until $t = 10$ s, then falls linearly to zero at $t = 14$ s. How far does the train travel in the full $14$ s? Give the answer in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: displacement is the area under the $v$-$t$ curve, $x = \int v\,dt$. The shape is a trapezoid: two triangles and a rectangle. $\tfrac12(4)(12) + (6)(12) + \tfrac12(4)(12) = 24 + 72 + 24 = 120$ m.

name: Area under an acceleration-time graph
statement: A cart starts from rest. Its acceleration is $+3.0$ m/s$^2$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 5.0$ s, then $-2.0$ m/s$^2$ from $t = 5.0$ s to $t = 11.0$ s. What is the cart's velocity at $t = 11.0$ s, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: $\Delta v = \int a\,dt$, the signed area under the $a$-$t$ graph. First segment: $(3.0)(5.0) = 15$ m/s. Second: $(-2.0)(6.0) = -12$ m/s. Starting from rest, $v = 15 - 12 = 3.0$ m/s.

name: Work as area under a force-position graph
statement: A block is pushed along a straight track. The applied force is along the motion and rises linearly from $0$ to $20$ N over the first $3.0$ m, then stays at $20$ N until $x = 8.0$ m. How much work does the force do over the $8.0$ m? Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: $W = \int F\,dx$ is the area under the $F$-$x$ graph. Triangle: $\tfrac12(3.0)(20) = 30$ J. Rectangle: $(5.0)(20) = 100$ J. Total $W = 130$ J.

name: Work to stretch a spring
statement: A spring obeys $F = kx$ with $k = 250$ N/m. How much work must you do to stretch it from its natural length to $x = 0.12$ m? Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: $W = \int_0^{x} kx'\,dx' = \tfrac12 kx^2$. So $W = \tfrac12(250)(0.12)^2 = 1.8$ J.

name: From a(t) to v(t)
statement: A particle starts from rest at $t = 0$ with acceleration $a(t) = 6t$ (SI units, $t$ in seconds). What is its speed at $t = 4.0$ s, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: $v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a\,dt'$. Here $v(t) = \int_0^t 6t'\,dt' = 3t^2$, so $v(4) = 3(16) = 48$ m/s.

name: Total charge from a ramping current
statement: The current through a wire grows as $i(t) = 0.40t$ amperes, with $t$ in seconds. How much total charge passes a cross-section between $t = 0$ and $t = 10$ s? Give the answer in coulombs.
solution: KEY IDEA: charge is the integral of current, $q = \int i\,dt$. $q = \int_0^{10} 0.40t\,dt = 0.20t^2\big|_0^{10} = 20$ C.

name: Impulse from a growing force
statement: During a collision the force on a ball grows linearly as $F(t) = 50t$ newtons for $0 \le t \le 0.20$ s, then drops to zero. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered, in N$\cdot$s?
solution: KEY IDEA: impulse $J = \int F\,dt$. $J = \int_0^{0.2} 50t\,dt = 25t^2\big|_0^{0.2} = 25(0.04) = 1.0$ N$\cdot$s.

name: Work by a quadratic force
statement: A force along the $x$-axis has magnitude $F(x) = 8.0x^2$ newtons, with $x$ in meters. How much work does it do on an object moved from $x = 0$ to $x = 3.0$ m? Give the answer in joules.

name: Center of mass of a rod with linear density
statement: A thin rod of length $2.0$ m lies along the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 2.0$ m. Its linear mass density grows in proportion to distance from the left end: $\lambda(x) = cx$. How far from the left end is the center of mass, in meters?
solution: KEY IDEA: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\int x\,\lambda\,dx}{\int \lambda\,dx}$. The constant $c$ cancels: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\int_0^L x^2 dx}{\int_0^L x\,dx} = \dfrac{L^3/3}{L^2/2} = \tfrac{2}{3}L = 1.33$ m.

name: RMS of a sinusoidal voltage
statement: A household voltage varies as $V(t) = 170\sin(\omega t)$ volts. The RMS value is defined by $V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^{T} V^2\,dt$ over one full period $T$. What is $V_{rms}$, in volts?
solution: KEY IDEA: the average of $\sin^2$ over a whole cycle is exactly $\tfrac12$. So $V_{rms}^2 = \tfrac12(170)^2$ and $V_{rms} = 170/\sqrt{2} = 120$ V.

name: Two integrations of a linear acceleration
statement: A cart starts from rest at the origin at $t = 0$ with acceleration $a(t) = 12 - 4t$ (SI units). How far from the origin is it at $t = 3.0$ s? Give the answer in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: integrate twice. $v(t) = \int_0^t (12 - 4t')dt' = 12t - 2t^2$, then $x(t) = \int_0^t v\,dt' = 6t^2 - \tfrac23 t^3$. At $t = 3$: $x = 54 - 18 = 36$ m.

name: Raising a satellite to twice the Earth's radius
statement: A $1200$ kg satellite is moved from the Earth's surface ($R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m) out to a radius of $2R$. Using $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$, how much work must be done against gravity? Ignore the Earth's rotation and any kinetic energy. Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: gravity weakens with distance, so $W = \int_R^{2R}\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}dr = GMm\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{2R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$. That gives $\dfrac{(3.986\times10^{14})(1200)}{2(6.37\times10^{6})} = 3.75\times10^{10}$ J.

name: Energy stored in a charging capacitor
statement: A $4.7\ \mu$F capacitor is charged from $0$ to $200$ V by a supply. The work to push the next increment of charge is $dW = (q/C)\,dq$. How much total energy ends up stored in the capacitor? Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: $W = \int_0^{Q}\dfrac{q}{C}dq = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C} = \tfrac12 CV^2$, since the voltage rises as the charge accumulates. $W = \tfrac12(4.7\times10^{-6})(200)^2 = 0.094$ J.

name: Lifting a chain off the floor
statement: A uniform chain of length $8.0$ m and mass per length $2.0$ kg/m lies coiled on the floor. You lift one end straight up until the whole chain hangs vertically, with its lower end just touching the floor. How much work do you do? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: the piece of chain that ends up at height $x$ has mass $\lambda\,dx$ and needs work $\lambda g x\,dx$. So $W = \int_0^{L}\lambda g x\,dx = \tfrac12 \lambda g L^2 = \tfrac12(2.0)(9.8)(64) = 627$ J. Equivalently, the center of mass rises to $L/2$.

name: Pumping a cylindrical tank dry
statement: An open cylindrical tank of radius $1.5$ m is filled with water to a depth of $3.0$ m, right up to the rim. Water has density $1000$ kg/m$^3$. How much work is needed to pump all of it out over the rim? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: a slab at height $y$ above the bottom has mass $\rho \pi r^2\,dy$ and must be raised $(3 - y)$. $W = \rho g \pi r^2 \int_0^{3}(3-y)\,dy = \rho g \pi r^2 (4.5)$. With $r = 1.5$ m this is $(1000)(9.8)\pi(2.25)(4.5) = 3.12\times10^{5}$ J.

name: Using v dv = a dx
statement: A bead starts from rest at $x = 0$ and its acceleration depends on position as $a(x) = 5.0x$ (SI units). What is its speed at $x = 4.0$ m, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: when $a$ is given as a function of $x$, use $v\,dv = a\,dx$. Then $\tfrac12 v^2 = \int_0^{4} 5x\,dx = \tfrac52 x^2\big|_0^4 = 40$, so $v = \sqrt{80} = 8.94$ m/s.

name: Moment of inertia of a rod about its end
statement: A uniform thin rod has mass $3.0$ kg and length $1.2$ m. Find its moment of inertia about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod, by integrating. Give the answer in kg$\cdot$m$^2$.
solution: KEY IDEA: $I = \int r^2\,dm$ with $dm = (M/L)dx$. $I = \dfrac{M}{L}\int_0^{L} x^2 dx = \dfrac{ML^2}{3} = \dfrac{(3.0)(1.44)}{3} = 1.44$ kg$\cdot$m$^2$.

name: Coasting boat with linear drag
statement: A $1200$ kg boat moving at $6.0$ m/s cuts its engine. The water exerts a drag force $F = -bv$ with $b = 90$ N$\cdot$s/m. How far does the boat coast before (asymptotically) stopping? Give the answer in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: write $m v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -bv$, so $m\,dv = -b\,dx$. Integrating from $v_0$ to $0$ gives $x = \dfrac{m v_0}{b} = \dfrac{(1200)(6.0)}{90} = 80$ m. The boat never truly stops, but the total distance is finite.

name: Triangular acceleration pulse
statement: A rocket sled starts from rest. Its acceleration rises linearly from $0$ to $6.0$ m/s$^2$ over $0 \le t \le 3.0$ s, then falls linearly back to zero at $t = 5.0$ s. What is its speed at $t = 5.0$ s, in m/s?
solution: KEY IDEA: $\Delta v$ is the area under the $a$-$t$ graph, here two triangles. $\tfrac12(3.0)(6.0) + \tfrac12(2.0)(6.0) = 9.0 + 6.0 = 15$ m/s.

name: Work by an inverse-square-like force
statement: A repulsive force along the $x$-axis has magnitude $F(x) = \dfrac{200}{(1 + x)^2}$ newtons, with $x$ in meters. How much work does it do on a bead pushed from $x = 0$ to $x = 3.0$ m? Give the answer in joules.

name: Impulse from a half-sine force pulse
statement: A bat strikes a ball with a force that follows $F(t) = 80\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{T}\right)$ newtons for $0 \le t \le T$, where $T = 0.50$ s, and is zero otherwise. What is the magnitude of the impulse, in N$\cdot$s?
solution: KEY IDEA: $J = \int_0^{T} F_0 \sin(\pi t/T)\,dt = \dfrac{2F_0 T}{\pi}$. With $F_0 = 80$ N and $T = 0.50$ s, $J = \dfrac{2(80)(0.5)}{\pi} = 25.5$ N$\cdot$s.

name: Center of mass with quadratic density
statement: A rod of length $1.00$ m lies from $x = 0$ to $x = 1.00$ m with linear density $\lambda(x) = \lambda_0\left(1 + x^2\right)$, where $x$ is in meters. Where is its center of mass, in meters from the left end?
solution: KEY IDEA: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\int_0^1 x(1+x^2)dx}{\int_0^1 (1+x^2)dx} = \dfrac{1/2 + 1/4}{1 + 1/3} = \dfrac{0.75}{1.3333} = 0.563$ m. It sits right of center because the rod is heavier on the right.

name: Rocket speed with shrinking mass
statement: A rocket in deep space (ignore gravity) has initial mass $3000$ kg and burns fuel at a steady $15$ kg/s while its engine produces a constant thrust of $45{,}000$ N. Starting from rest, what is its speed after a $60$ s burn? Give the answer in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: the acceleration is not constant because the mass shrinks: $a(t) = \dfrac{F}{m_0 - kt}$. Then $v = \int_0^{t_b}\dfrac{F\,dt}{m_0 - kt} = \dfrac{F}{k}\ln\!\dfrac{m_0}{m_0 - kt_b}$. With $m_0 - kt_b = 3000 - 900 = 2100$ kg, $v = 3000\ln(3000/2100) = 1.07\times10^{3}$ m/s.

name: Chain sliding off a table
statement: A uniform chain of total length $6.0$ m and total mass $12$ kg lies on a frictionless table with $2.0$ m hanging over the edge. It is released from rest and slides off. How fast is it moving the instant the last link leaves the table? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: track the potential energy of the hanging part, whose center of mass is $h/2$ below the edge: $U(h) = -\lambda g h^2/2$ with $\lambda = 2.0$ kg/m. From $h = 2$ to $h = 6$, $|\Delta U| = \tfrac12(2.0)(9.8)(36 - 4) = 313.6$ J. Then $v = \sqrt{2(313.6)/12} = 7.23$ m/s.

name: Pumping a conical tank
statement: A tank is a cone with its apex pointing down, height $4.0$ m and top radius $2.0$ m. It is full of water ($1000$ kg/m$^3$). How much work is required to pump all the water out over the top rim? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: at height $y$ above the apex, the cross-section has radius $r = y/2$, so a slab has volume $\pi y^2/4\,dy$ and must rise $(4-y)$. $W = \rho g \dfrac{\pi}{4}\int_0^{4} y^2(4-y)\,dy = \rho g \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{4\cdot 64}{3} - \dfrac{256}{4}\right) = \rho g (16.76)$, giving $1.64\times10^{5}$ J.

name: Work to reach a 500 km orbit altitude
statement: How much work must be done against gravity to raise a $500$ kg payload from the Earth's surface ($R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m) to an altitude of $500$ km? Use $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$ and neglect kinetic energy and air resistance. Give the answer in joules.
solution: KEY IDEA: $W = \int_{R}^{R+h}\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}dr = GMm\left(\dfrac1R - \dfrac{1}{R+h}\right)$. With $R+h = 6.87\times10^{6}$ m, $W = (3.986\times10^{14})(500)(1.5699\times10^{-7} - 1.4556\times10^{-7}) = 2.28\times10^{9}$ J. Note $mgh$ would give $2.45\times10^{9}$ J, about 8% high.

name: Moment of inertia of a disk with graded density
statement: A flat disk of radius $0.50$ m and total mass $2.0$ kg has an areal density that grows with radius as $\sigma(r) = \sigma_0 r$. Find its moment of inertia about the central axis perpendicular to the disk, in kg$\cdot$m$^2$.
solution: KEY IDEA: use rings, $dm = \sigma_0 r(2\pi r\,dr)$. Then $M = 2\pi\sigma_0 R^3/3$ and $I = \int r^2 dm = 2\pi\sigma_0 R^5/5$. Dividing, $I = \tfrac35 MR^2 = 0.6(2.0)(0.25) = 0.30$ kg$\cdot$m$^2$ — larger than $\tfrac12 MR^2$ because mass sits farther out.

name: Distance to halve speed under quadratic drag
statement: A skydiver of mass $80$ kg moving horizontally at high speed feels only a drag force $F = -cv^2$ with $c = 0.25$ kg/m (ignore gravity for this horizontal glide). Over what distance does the speed drop to half its initial value? Give the answer in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: $m v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -cv^2$ gives $\dfrac{dv}{v} = -\dfrac{c}{m}dx$. Integrating, $x = \dfrac{m}{c}\ln\!\dfrac{v_0}{v} = \dfrac{80}{0.25}\ln 2 = 222$ m. Notice the answer does not depend on $v_0$.

name: Burnout altitude of a rocket fighting gravity
statement: A rocket lifts off vertically from rest with initial mass $6000$ kg, exhaust speed $u = 2500$ m/s, and a steady burn rate of $40$ kg/s for $100$ s. Its speed obeys $v(t) = u\ln\!\dfrac{m_0}{m_0 - kt} - gt$. Ignoring air resistance and taking $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$ constant, what altitude does it reach at burnout? Give the answer in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: altitude is $\int_0^{t_b} v\,dt$, and the logarithm integrates to $\int_0^{t_b}\ln\frac{m_0}{m_0-kt}dt = t_b + \dfrac{m_f}{k}\ln\dfrac{m_f}{m_0}$ with $m_f = 2000$ kg. That gives $u\left(100 + 50\ln\tfrac{2000}{6000}\right) - \tfrac12 g t_b^2 = 2500(45.07) - 49000 \approx 6.37\times10^{4}$ m.

name: Falling to Earth from three radii out
statement: A small object is released from rest at a distance $3R$ from the Earth's center, where $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m. Neglecting air resistance and the Moon, how fast is it moving when it reaches the Earth's surface? Use $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$. Give the answer in m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: gravity is not constant over this distance, so integrate the force: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = \int_{R}^{3R}\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}dr = GMm\left(\dfrac1R - \dfrac{1}{3R}\right) = \dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$. Then $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{4GM}{3R}} = \sqrt{8.34\times10^{7}} = 9.13\times10^{3}$ m/s, just below escape speed.

name: Restoring force on a small-angle pendulum
statement: A pendulum bob of mass $0.25$ kg hangs on a light string. The string is displaced $4.0^\circ$ from vertical. Using the small-angle approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ (with $\theta$ in radians), find the magnitude of the restoring force along the arc, in newtons.
solution: KEY IDEA: the tangential force is $mg\sin\theta$, and for small $\theta$ in radians $\sin\theta\approx\theta$. Convert: $4.0^\circ = 0.0698$ rad. Then $F \approx mg\theta = (0.25)(9.8)(0.0698) = 0.171$ N. The exact value $mg\sin\theta = 0.1709$ N differs by less than $0.1\%$.

name: Gravity at 250 km altitude
statement: The gravitational field strength at height $h$ above Earth's surface is $g(h) = g_0\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)^{-2}$ with $R = 6.37\times10^6$ m. Use the binomial approximation $(1+x)^n \approx 1+nx$ to estimate the percent decrease in $g$ at $h = 250$ km. Give the answer in percent.
solution: KEY IDEA: with $x = h/R = 250/6370 = 0.03925 \ll 1$, $(1+x)^{-2} \approx 1-2x$. The fractional decrease is $2h/R = 0.0785$, i.e. $7.85\%$. (The exact value is $7.41\%$; the first-order estimate overshoots slightly because $x$ is not tiny.)

name: Fractional change in pendulum period
statement: A pendulum's length is increased by $0.60\%$. Using $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ and the binomial approximation, find the percent increase in the period.
solution: KEY IDEA: $T \propto L^{1/2}$, so writing $L \to L(1+x)$ gives $T \to T(1+x)^{1/2} \approx T(1+x/2)$. With $x = 0.0060$, $\Delta T/T = 0.0030 = 0.30\%$. Half-power laws always halve a small fractional change.

name: Fraction of a sample decayed in a short time
statement: A radioactive sample has half-life $12.0$ hours. Use $e^{-x} \approx 1-x$ for small $x$ to estimate the fraction of nuclei that decay in the first $6.0$ minutes. Give a dimensionless number.
solution: KEY IDEA: the surviving fraction is $e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda = \ln 2/t_{1/2}$, so the decayed fraction is $1-e^{-\lambda t} \approx \lambda t$ when $\lambda t \ll 1$. Here $\lambda t = (\ln 2)(0.100\ \text{h})/(12.0\ \text{h}) = 5.78\times10^{-3}$. The exact answer, $5.76\times10^{-3}$, is within $0.3\%$.

name: How high does the bob rise?
statement: A pendulum of length $1.20$ m swings to a maximum angle of $6.0^\circ$ from vertical. Use $\cos\theta \approx 1-\theta^2/2$ to estimate how high the bob rises above its lowest point, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: the rise is $h = L(1-\cos\theta)$, and the leading term of $1-\cos\theta$ is $\theta^2/2$, not $\theta$. With $\theta = 0.1047$ rad, $h \approx L\theta^2/2 = (1.20)(0.01097)/2 = 6.58\times10^{-3}$ m. Note that the first-order term vanishes, so you must keep the quadratic term.

name: Gamma factor for a slow particle
statement: An electron moves at $v = 0.010c$. Use the binomial approximation on $\gamma = (1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ to estimate $\gamma - 1$. Give a dimensionless number.
solution: KEY IDEA: with $x = -v^2/c^2$ and $n = -1/2$, $\gamma \approx 1 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2}$. So $\gamma - 1 \approx \frac{1}{2}(0.010)^2 = 5.0\times10^{-5}$. The exact value agrees to four digits.

name: Area expansion of a metal plate
statement: An aluminum plate ($\alpha = 2.4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$) is heated by $80$ K. Each linear dimension grows by the factor $(1+\alpha\Delta T)$. Use the binomial approximation to find the fractional increase in the plate's area. Give a dimensionless number.
solution: KEY IDEA: area scales as the square of a length, so $A \to A(1+\alpha\Delta T)^2 \approx A(1+2\alpha\Delta T)$. Thus $\Delta A/A \approx 2(2.4\times10^{-5})(80) = 3.84\times10^{-3}$. The dropped term $(\alpha\Delta T)^2 \approx 3.7\times10^{-6}$ is negligible.

name: Pendulum taken to a place with weaker gravity
statement: A pendulum clock is moved to a location where $g$ is smaller by $0.30\%$. By what percent does its period increase?
solution: KEY IDEA: $T \propto g^{-1/2}$, so $\Delta T/T \approx -\frac{1}{2}\Delta g/g$. A $0.30\%$ decrease in $g$ gives a $0.15\%$ increase in period. The clock runs slow by that fraction.

name: Laser spot shift from a small tilt
statement: A laser is aimed at a wall $8.0$ m away and then tilted by $0.25^\circ$. Use $\tan\theta \approx \theta$ to find how far the spot moves along the wall, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: the displacement is $d = L\tan\theta \approx L\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians. Here $\theta = 0.25^\circ = 4.363\times10^{-3}$ rad, so $d \approx (8.0)(4.363\times10^{-3}) = 0.0349$ m, about $3.5$ cm. At this angle $\tan\theta$ and $\theta$ agree to six digits.

name: Refraction at a small angle of incidence
statement: Light strikes a flat water surface ($n = 1.33$) at $3.0^\circ$ from the normal. Using $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ on both sides of Snell's law, find the refraction angle in the water, in degrees.
solution: KEY IDEA: Snell's law is $\sin\theta_1 = n\sin\theta_2$; for small angles this becomes $\theta_1 \approx n\theta_2$, and because the approximation is linear the angles may be left in degrees. So $\theta_2 \approx 3.0/1.33 = 2.26^\circ$, matching the exact result to three digits.

name: Second-order correction to kinetic energy
statement: A particle moves at $v = 0.050c$. Expanding $K = (\gamma-1)mc^2$ to the next order beyond $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ gives $K \approx \frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1+\frac{3}{4}\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)$. By what fraction does the true kinetic energy exceed the Newtonian value? Give a dimensionless number.
solution: KEY IDEA: keep two terms of $\gamma = 1 + \frac{1}{2}\beta^2 + \frac{3}{8}\beta^4 + \dots$, so $K = mc^2(\frac{1}{2}\beta^2 + \frac{3}{8}\beta^4)$ and the fractional excess over $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is $\frac{3}{4}\beta^2$. With $\beta = 0.050$, that is $\frac{3}{4}(0.0025) = 1.88\times10^{-3}$. Direct evaluation of $\gamma$ confirms $1.879\times10^{-3}$.

name: Tidal acceleration from the Moon
statement: The Moon ($M = 7.35\times10^{22}$ kg) is $d = 3.84\times10^{8}$ m from Earth's center. Expanding $GM/(d\mp R)^2$ to first order in $R/d$, the tidal acceleration at the sublunar point relative to Earth's center is $2GMR/d^3$. Compute it, with $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m and $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: KEY IDEA: the tide comes from the *difference* in field across Earth, and that difference is the derivative $\frac{d}{dr}(GM/r^2)\,\Delta r = -2GM R/d^3$ — a binomial expansion in disguise. Numerically $2(6.674\times10^{-11})(7.35\times10^{22})(6.37\times10^{6})/(3.84\times10^{8})^3 = 1.10\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, about $10^{-7}$ of $g$.

name: When does mgh stop working?
statement: The exact gravitational potential energy is $U = -GM_Em/r$. Rising a height $h$ from the surface changes it by $\Delta U = GM_Em\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{R+h}\right)$. Expanding in $h/R$ gives $\Delta U \approx mgh(1 - h/R)$. For $h = 10.0$ km and $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m, by what percent does $mgh$ overestimate the true energy change?
solution: KEY IDEA: factor the exact expression as $\frac{GM_Em h}{R^2}\left(1+h/R\right)^{-1} \approx mgh(1-h/R)$. The fractional overestimate of $mgh$ is therefore just $h/R = 10.0/6370 = 1.57\times10^{-3}$, or $0.157\%$. This is why $mgh$ is safe for laboratory heights and unsafe for orbits.

name: Precision of a g measurement
statement: A student finds $g$ from $g = 4\pi^2 L/T^2$. The length is known to $\pm 0.20\%$ and the period to $\pm 0.10\%$. Using a first-order Taylor expansion to propagate the errors (worst case, adding magnitudes), what is the percent uncertainty in $g$?
solution: KEY IDEA: for a product of powers, $\frac{\delta g}{g} = \frac{\delta L}{L} + 2\frac{\delta T}{T}$ — each exponent multiplies its fractional error. That gives $0.20\% + 2(0.10\%) = 0.40\%$. The period matters twice as much per percent, which is why one times many swings at once.

name: Deviation by a thin prism
statement: A thin glass prism has apex angle $A = 5.0^\circ$ and index $n = 1.52$. For small angles, applying $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ at both faces gives a deviation $\delta = (n-1)A$. Find $\delta$ in degrees.
solution: KEY IDEA: at each face Snell's law linearizes to $\theta_1 = n\theta_2$, and the geometry gives total deviation $\delta = \theta_1+\theta_1' - A$. Combining with $\theta_2+\theta_2' = A$ yields $\delta = (n-1)A$, independent of how the ray enters. Numerically $\delta = 0.52 \times 5.0^\circ = 2.6^\circ$.

name: Sag of a nearly straight cable
statement: A uniform cable of linear density $1.5$ kg/m is strung horizontally across a $40.0$ m span under a tension of $5.0\times10^{3}$ N. For small sag the catenary reduces to the parabola $y = \mu g x^2/(2T)$ measured from the lowest point. Find the sag at the center, in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: expanding $\cosh(\mu g x/T)\approx 1+\frac{1}{2}(\mu g x/T)^2$ turns the catenary into a parabola whenever the sag is small compared with the span. With $x = 20.0$ m (half the span), $s = (1.5)(9.8)(20.0)^2/(2\times5.0\times10^3) = 0.588$ m. The sag is $1.5\%$ of the span, so the approximation is excellent.

name: Raising a satellite by ten kilometers
statement: A satellite orbits at an altitude of $400$ km ($r = 6.77\times10^{6}$ m), where its period is $5.54\times10^{3}$ s. Kepler's third law gives $T \propto r^{3/2}$. Use the binomial approximation to find how much the period increases if the orbital radius is raised by $10.0$ km, in seconds.
solution: KEY IDEA: $T \propto r^{3/2}$ implies $\Delta T/T \approx \frac{3}{2}\Delta r/r$. Here $\Delta r/r = 10.0/6770 = 1.477\times10^{-3}$, so $\Delta T/T = 2.216\times10^{-3}$ and $\Delta T = (5.54\times10^3)(2.216\times10^{-3}) = 12.3$ s. Recomputing the period exactly gives the same value.

name: Redshift of a receding star
statement: A star recedes at $v = 3.00\times10^{5}$ m/s. For $v \ll c$ the relativistic Doppler formula reduces to $\Delta\lambda/\lambda \approx v/c$. Find the shift of the hydrogen line at $\lambda = 656.3$ nm, in nanometers. Take $c = 3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: $\lambda' = \lambda\sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}} \approx \lambda(1+\beta)$ once both square roots are expanded to first order. With $\beta = 1.00\times10^{-3}$, $\Delta\lambda = (656.3)(1.00\times10^{-3}) = 0.656$ nm. The second-order term would add only about $3\times10^{-4}$ nm.

name: Length contraction of an airliner
statement: An airliner of proper length $60.0$ m flies at $250$ m/s. Using $\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2} \approx 1-\frac{v^2}{2c^2}$, find how much shorter it is in the ground frame, in meters. Take $c = 3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: the contraction is $\Delta L = L\left(1-\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\right) \approx L\beta^2/2$. With $\beta^2 = (250/3.00\times10^8)^2 = 6.94\times10^{-13}$, $\Delta L = (60.0)(3.47\times10^{-13}) = 2.08\times10^{-11}$ m — smaller than an atom. Trying to evaluate $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ on a calculator directly would return exactly 1.

name: Pressure one hundred meters up
statement: In an isothermal atmosphere $p = p_0 e^{-h/H}$ with scale height $H = 8500$ m. Take $p_0 = 101.3$ kPa and use $e^{-x} \approx 1-x$ to estimate the pressure at the top of a $100$ m tower, in kilopascals.
solution: KEY IDEA: for $h \ll H$ the exponential is linear, $p \approx p_0(1-h/H)$, which is just the hydrostatic result $p_0 - \rho g h$. With $h/H = 0.01176$, $p \approx 101.3(1-0.01176) = 100.1$ kPa. The exact exponential gives $100.12$ kPa.

name: Field of a distant dipole
statement: Two charges $+2.0$ nC and $-2.0$ nC are separated by $2.0$ mm along the $x$-axis. On the axis at $x = 0.50$ m from the center, expanding $\frac{1}{(x\mp d/2)^2}$ in powers of $d/x$ gives $E \approx \frac{2kp}{x^3}$ with $p = qd$. Compute $E$ in N/C, using $k = 8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$.
solution: KEY IDEA: the monopole terms cancel exactly, so the leading surviving term comes from the first-order binomial expansion, and the field falls off as $1/x^3$ rather than $1/x^2$. With $p = (2.0\times10^{-9})(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 4.0\times10^{-12}$ C\,m, $E = 2(8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-12})/(0.50)^3 = 0.575$ N/C.

name: Pendulum clock in a warm room
statement: A pendulum clock with a brass rod ($\alpha = 1.9\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$) is calibrated at $20^\circ$C. The room warms to $35^\circ$C. Using $T \propto L^{1/2}$ and the binomial approximation, how many seconds does the clock lose in one day?
solution: KEY IDEA: $\Delta L/L = \alpha\Delta T$, and the half-power gives $\Delta T/T = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta T$. That is $\frac{1}{2}(1.9\times10^{-5})(15) = 1.425\times10^{-4}$. Over $86400$ s the clock falls behind by $(1.425\times10^{-4})(86400) = 12.3$ s.

name: Amplitude correction to a pendulum clock
statement: The period of a pendulum swung to amplitude $\theta_0$ is $T = T_0\left(1+\frac{\theta_0^2}{16}+\dots\right)$, where $T_0 = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ is the small-angle result. A clock is regulated assuming $T_0$ but actually swings to $\theta_0 = 20^\circ$. How many seconds does it lose per day?
solution: KEY IDEA: the leading correction is quadratic in amplitude, so it comes from the $\theta^3$ term of $\sin\theta$ that the small-angle approximation throws away. With $\theta_0 = 0.3491$ rad, $\theta_0^2/16 = 7.615\times10^{-3}$. Over $86400$ s that is $(7.615\times10^{-3})(86400) = 658$ s, about eleven minutes — small-angle errors are not always small.

name: Vibration frequency in a Lennard-Jones well
statement: Two atoms interact through $U(r) = U_0\left[\left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^{12}-2\left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^{6}\right]$, which has its minimum at $r = a$. Expanding $U$ to second order about $r = a$ gives an effective spring constant $k = 72U_0/a^2$. For $U_0 = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ J, $a = 3.0\times10^{-10}$ m, and reduced mass $m = 1.0\times10^{-26}$ kg, find the angular frequency of small vibrations, in rad/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: near a minimum every potential looks like a parabola: $U \approx U_{\min} + \frac{1}{2}U''(a)(r-a)^2$, so $k = U''(a)$. Differentiating twice gives $U''(a) = 72U_0/a^2 = 72(1.6\times10^{-19})/(9.0\times10^{-20}) = 128$ N/m. Then $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{128/1.0\times10^{-26}} = 1.13\times10^{14}$ rad/s, an infrared vibration.

name: Height of the equilibrium tide
statement: Balancing the Moon's tidal potential against Earth's own gravity gives an equilibrium tidal bulge of height $h = \frac{3}{2}\frac{M_m}{M_E}\frac{R^4}{d^3}$. With $M_m = 7.35\times10^{22}$ kg, $M_E = 5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m, and $d = 3.84\times10^{8}$ m, compute $h$ in meters.
solution: KEY IDEA: the tidal potential is the second-order term left over after expanding $-GM_m/|\vec{d}-\vec{r}|$ in powers of $R/d$; setting that equal to $gh$ on Earth's surface gives the formula above. Numerically $\frac{3}{2}(0.01231)(1.647\times10^{27})/(5.66\times10^{25}) = 0.54$ m. Real tides differ from this because ocean basins resonate.

name: Tidal stretch on an astronaut
statement: An astronaut of height $1.8$ m floats in a spacecraft at orbital radius $r = 6.77\times10^{6}$ m, oriented radially. Using the first-order expansion of $GM_E/r^2$, find the difference in gravitational acceleration between the astronaut's head and feet, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Take $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$.
solution: KEY IDEA: differentiate the field rather than subtracting two nearly equal numbers: $|\Delta a| = \frac{2GM_E}{r^3}\Delta r$. With $\Delta r = 1.8$ m, $|\Delta a| = 2(3.986\times10^{14})(1.8)/(3.10\times10^{20}) = 4.6\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Subtracting the two accelerations directly would lose all significant figures on a calculator.

name: Counting Newton's rings
statement: A plano-convex lens of radius of curvature $2.00$ m rests on a flat glass plate. The air gap a distance $r$ from the contact point is $t = r^2/2R$, which follows from expanding $R-\sqrt{R^2-r^2}$. Illuminated from above with $589$ nm light, how many dark rings appear within a radius of $1.00$ cm? Give an integer.
solution: KEY IDEA: $\sqrt{R^2-r^2} = R\sqrt{1-r^2/R^2} \approx R(1-r^2/2R^2)$, so the gap is $t = r^2/2R$. Dark rings occur where $2t = m\lambda$, i.e. $m = r^2/(R\lambda)$. At $r = 1.00$ cm, $t = 2.50\times10^{-5}$ m and $m = 2t/\lambda = 84.9$, so $84$ complete dark rings fit inside.

name: How large an amplitude is still small?
statement: Using $T = T_0(1+\theta_0^2/16)$, find the largest amplitude for which the small-angle period is accurate to $0.10\%$. Give the answer in degrees.
solution: KEY IDEA: set the fractional error equal to the tolerance: $\theta_0^2/16 = 1.0\times10^{-3}$, so $\theta_0 = \sqrt{0.016} = 0.1265$ rad. Converting, $\theta_0 = 7.2^\circ$. This is the practical rule that pendulum swings under roughly $7^\circ$ are isochronous to a part in a thousand.

name: Why GPS clocks need a correction
statement: A GPS satellite orbits at $r = 2.656\times10^{7}$ m. Two first-order effects shift its clock rate relative to a clock on Earth's surface ($R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m): the gravitational shift $\frac{GM_E}{c^2}\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{r}\right)$ makes it run fast, and the kinematic shift $\frac{v^2}{2c^2}$ with $v^2 = GM_E/r$ makes it run slow. Find the net time the satellite clock gains per day, in microseconds. Use $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and $c = 3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s.
solution: KEY IDEA: both effects are first-order expansions of square roots in $\Phi/c^2$ and $v^2/c^2$, so they simply add. The gravitational term is $5.285\times10^{-10}$ and the kinematic term is $8.34\times10^{-11}$, giving a net fractional rate of $4.45\times10^{-10}$. Over $86400$ s that is $(4.45\times10^{-10})(86400) = 38.5\ \mu$s — uncorrected, this would push GPS positions off by more than $10$ km per day.

name: Deflection of a plumb line by Earth's rotation
statement: Because Earth rotates, a plumb bob at latitude $\lambda$ hangs slightly off the true radial direction. The centrifugal acceleration $\omega^2R\cos\lambda$ has a horizontal component $\omega^2R\cos\lambda\sin\lambda$, and for a small deflection $\tan\delta \approx \delta$. Find the deflection at $\lambda = 45^\circ$, in degrees. Take $\omega = 7.292\times10^{-5}$ rad/s, $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m, $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: KEY IDEA: the deflection satisfies $\tan\delta = \frac{\omega^2R\sin\lambda\cos\lambda}{g}$, and at $45^\circ$ the product $\sin\lambda\cos\lambda = 1/2$. Then $\delta \approx \omega^2R/(2g) = (5.317\times10^{-9})(6.37\times10^{6})/19.6 = 1.728\times10^{-3}$ rad. Converting, $\delta = 0.099^\circ$, or about $6$ arcminutes — the maximum anywhere on Earth.

name: Tilted Axes on a Frictionless Incline
statement: A $2.0\,\text{kg}$ block slides on a frictionless incline of angle $\theta = 30^\circ$. Find the magnitude of its acceleration along the incline, in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: KEY IDEA: tilt the axes so $x$ points down the slope. Then the normal force has no $x$ component and the motion is one-dimensional in $x$. Newton's law along the slope gives $ma = mg\sin\theta$, so $a = g\sin 30^\circ = 4.9\,\text{m/s}^2$. The mass cancels, which is the usual sign that the axis choice was right.

name: Normal Force with Tilted Axes
statement: The same $2.0\,\text{kg}$ block sits on a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline. Using axes along and perpendicular to the surface, find the normal force in $\text{N}$.
